Description: A framework enabling teams to launch application-specific Arbitrum chains (Orbit chains) that settle to Ethereum via Arbitrum (L2 or L3), inheriting Arbitrum’s optimistic execution and settlement model.
Reason of inclusion: Provides standardized rollup/appchain deployment templates (execution, settlement, security) that allow teams to launch Ethereum-anchored chains without bespoke protocol engineering.
Practitioner's Note: Orbit should be evaluated as a scaling deployment abstraction on top of Arbitrum Nitro, not as a standalone rollup. Design choices largely inherit Arbitrum’s optimistic assumptions.
Practitioner Validation Check: If Orbit were removed, teams would need to rebuild Arbitrum-compatible rollup logic to launch Arbitrum-anchored appchains.
Level of Protocol Abstraction: High — standardized deployment, configuration, and contracts.
Bespoke Engineering Required: Limited — application logic and configuration, not protocol design.
Configurable Parameters: Gas pricing, block times, fee models, sequencer operation, upgrade cadence.
Sequencer Model Options: Single sequencer by default; customization possible per deployment.
Upgrade Model: Per-chain upgrades by deployer, constrained by Nitro compatibility.
Settlement Layer: Ethereum L1 via Arbitrum (Orbit chains typically settle to Arbitrum, which settles to Ethereum).
Security Inheritance: Indirect Ethereum security; direct inheritance from Arbitrum’s optimistic model.
Fault / Validity Proof Inheritance: Inherits Arbitrum fraud-proof system and challenge assumptions.
Isolation vs Shared Security: Execution isolated per chain; settlement and security shared upstream.
Does This Enable L3s: Yes — Orbit commonly used for L3 appchains settling to Arbitrum.
Failure Propagation Model: L3 issues can cascade to L2 (Arbitrum) before reaching L1.
Latency Trade-offs: Lower fees and higher throughput at the cost of additional settlement hops.
Framework Ownership: Developed by Offchain Labs; ecosystem governed via Arbitrum DAO.
Who Controls Upgrades: Chain deployer controls appchain upgrades; core Nitro changes governed upstream.
Emergency Controls: Deployer-defined emergency controls; upstream Arbitrum safeguards apply.
Path to Sovereignty: Moderate — appchains retain operational control but depend on Arbitrum protocol evolution.
Operational Complexity: Medium — simpler than building a rollup from scratch; more complex than deploying on an L2.
Fixed vs Variable Costs: Fixed costs for sequencer/infrastructure; variable costs tied to usage and upstream fees.
Infrastructure Responsibility Split: Deployer manages chain ops; Arbitrum manages upstream protocol.
Vendor Lock-in Risk: Moderate — tight coupling to Arbitrum Nitro and ecosystem.
Number of Chains Deployed: Multiple Orbit chains live or announced across gaming, DeFi, and infra.
Types of Users: Application teams seeking custom execution environments.
Ecosystem Alignment: Strong alignment with Arbitrum ecosystem and tooling.
Dependency Concentration Risk: High dependency on Arbitrum’s roadmap and governance outcomes.
Native Interoperability Support: Best within Arbitrum ecosystem; no native cross-L2 standard.
Cross-Rollup Messaging Assumptions: Relies on bridges/messaging layers external to Orbit.
External Bridge Dependency: Yes — required for broader Ethereum and cross-rollup interoperability.

Entity: OP Stack (already used, but also belongs here contextually)
Description: A modular, open-source Optimistic Rollup framework that enables teams to deploy Ethereum-anchored L2s and L3s with standardized execution, settlement, and governance components.
Reason of inclusion: Defines a reusable rollup and appchain deployment standard that allows teams to launch Ethereum-settled chains without rebuilding optimistic rollup protocol logic.
Practitioner's Note: OP Stack should be evaluated as a rollup operating system, not a single chain. Its design choices propagate across all OP Stack–based chains (the Superchain).
Practitioner Validation Check: If OP Stack were removed, multiple Ethereum-anchored rollups and appchains would lose their execution framework, fraud-proof logic, and settlement standard.
Underlying Rollup Base: Native Optimistic Rollup design maintained by the Optimism ecosystem.
Level of Protocol Abstraction: High — standardized contracts, execution clients, and configuration templates.
Bespoke Engineering Required: Limited — teams configure parameters and infrastructure rather than designing protocol mechanics.
Execution Environment Options: EVM-equivalent (designed to closely mirror Ethereum L1 semantics).
Configurable Parameters: Gas pricing, block time, fee routing, sequencer setup, upgrade cadence.
Sequencer Model Options: Single sequencer by default; roadmap includes shared and decentralized sequencing.
Upgrade Model: Framework upgrades coordinated at the Superchain level; per-chain upgrades possible within constraints.
Security Inheritance: Full Ethereum settlement security via optimistic assumptions.
Fault / Validity Proof Inheritance: Inherits OP Stack fraud-proof system and challenge window assumptions.
Isolation vs Shared Security: Execution isolated per chain; security and settlement assumptions shared across OP Stack chains.
Does This Enable L3s: Yes — OP Stack supports L3-style deployments (e.g., appchains settling to OP-based L2s).
Base Layer Dependency: Ethereum L1 or OP Stack L2s (configurable).
Failure Propagation Model: L3 → L2 → L1, depending on deployment topology.
Latency Trade-offs: Improved throughput and lower fees with additional settlement hops.
Framework Ownership: Maintained by the Optimism ecosystem; governed by the Optimism Collective.
Who Controls Upgrades: Framework upgrades coordinated by Optimism governance; chain operators control local configuration.
Emergency Controls: Emergency pause and intervention mechanisms exist at both framework and chain levels.
Path to Sovereignty: Moderate — chains retain operational control but share core protocol evolution with the Superchain.
Operational Complexity: Medium — simpler than bespoke rollup design; requires infra management beyond standard L2 deployment.
Fixed vs Variable Costs: Fixed costs for sequencing and infra; variable costs driven by L1 data posting and usage.
Infrastructure Responsibility Split: Chain operators manage execution infra; Optimism maintains core framework.
Vendor Lock-in Risk: Moderate — tight coupling to OP Stack standards and Superchain governance.
Number of Chains Deployed: Multiple production chains (e.g., Base, Optimism, others in the Superchain).
Types of Users: Application teams, enterprises, and ecosystems seeking standardized Ethereum rollups.
Ecosystem Alignment: Strong alignment within the OP Superchain.
Dependency Concentration Risk: Shared framework risk across all OP Stack chains.
Native Interoperability Support: Designed for Superchain-native interoperability (shared standards and messaging assumptions).
Composability with Base Rollup: Asynchronous composability with Ethereum and Superchain peers.
Cross-Rollup Messaging Assumptions: Relies on standardized OP Stack messaging patterns.

Description: A modular ZK rollup and appchain framework that enables teams to deploy Ethereum-anchored ZK rollups, L3s, and validiums using shared proving, execution, and settlement standards.
Reason of inclusion: Defines standardized deployment templates, execution semantics, and settlement models that allow teams to launch ZK-based chains without bespoke protocol engineering.
Practitioner's Note: ZK Stack should be evaluated as a ZK-native rollup operating system: it emphasizes cryptographic finality, configurable DA models, and a multi-chain ecosystem rather than a single shared execution environment.
Practitioner Validation Check: If ZK Stack were removed, teams would need to rebuild ZK execution, proving pipelines, and Ethereum settlement logic to launch zkSync-style chains.
Underlying Rollup Base: zkSync ZK rollup architecture (SNARK-based validity proofs).
Level of Protocol Abstraction: High — standardized contracts, provers, and deployment workflows.
Bespoke Engineering Required: Limited — configuration and infra integration, not protocol design.
Configurable Parameters: DA mode (rollup vs validium), gas model, block times, fee routing, sequencer configuration.
Sequencer Model Options: Single sequencer per chain by default; decentralization models are roadmap-driven and configurable.
Upgrade Model: Framework-level upgrades coordinated by ZK Stack governance; per-chain upgrades possible within constraints.
Security Inheritance:
Configurable:
- Full Ethereum security for rollup deployments
- Partial security for validium deployments (off-chain DA)
Fault / Validity Proof Inheritance: Inherits ZK validity-proof system defined by ZK Stack.
Isolation vs Shared Security: Execution isolated per chain; proving and settlement standards shared.
Does This Enable L3s: Yes — explicitly supports L3-style zkChains settling to Ethereum (directly or via L2).
Base Layer Dependency: Ethereum L1; optional dependency on zkSync Era as an ecosystem hub.
Failure Propagation Model: L3 → L2 (if used) → L1, depending on deployment topology.
Latency Trade-offs: Lower fees and faster UX at the cost of additional settlement layers.
Framework Ownership: Developed and stewarded by Matter Labs, with ecosystem governance evolving over time.
Who Controls Upgrades: Framework upgrades governed centrally; chain deployers control local configuration.
Emergency Controls: Emergency pause and intervention mechanisms exist at framework and chain levels.
Path to Sovereignty: Moderate — chains gain operational control but remain coupled to ZK Stack evolution.
Operational Complexity: Medium–high — ZK proving infrastructure adds complexity relative to optimistic stacks.
Fixed vs Variable Costs: High fixed prover costs; variable costs scale with usage and L1 data posting.
Infrastructure Responsibility Split: Chain deployers manage infra; ZK Stack provides protocol and tooling.
Vendor Lock-in Risk: Moderate–high — tight coupling to ZK Stack tooling and Matter Labs roadmap.
Number of Chains Deployed: Growing number of zkChains and appchains built on ZK Stack.
Types of Users: Application teams, enterprises, and ecosystems requiring custom ZK execution.
Ecosystem Alignment: Strong alignment within the zkSync / ZK Stack ecosystem.
Dependency Concentration Risk: High dependency on ZK Stack governance and shared proving infrastructure.
Native Interoperability Support: Strongest within the ZK Stack ecosystem (shared standards and tooling).
Composability with Base Rollup: Asynchronous composability with Ethereum and zkSync-based chains.
Cross-Rollup Messaging Assumptions: Relies on standardized ZK Stack messaging patterns.
External Bridge Dependency: Required for interoperability outside the ZK Stack ecosystem.

Bespoke Engineering Required: Limited — teams primarily configure parameters and infrastructure.

Upgrade Model: Framework-level upgrades coordinated by Polygon; per-chain upgrades possible within constraints.
Security Inheritance:

- Partial security for validium-style deployments (off-chain DA)
Fault / Validity Proof Inheritance: Inherits SNARK-based validity-proof system defined by Polygon CDK.
Isolation vs Shared Security: Execution isolated per chain; proving and settlement standards shared.
Does This Enable L3s: Yes — supports L3-style zk appchains settling to Ethereum directly or via L2 hubs.

Failure Propagation Model: L3 → L2 (if used) → L1, depending on deployment topology.

Description: A high-performance appchain SDK developed by Avalanche that enables teams to build custom virtual machines and application-specific chains, including configurations that anchor settlement or security back to Ethereum.
Reason of inclusion: Provides a framework that allows teams to launch Ethereum-anchored appchains with custom execution environments without building chain logic from scratch, when configured for Ethereum settlement or security anchoring.
Practitioner's Note: HyperSDK should be evaluated as a maximum-flexibility appchain framework. Ethereum anchoring is optional and configuration-dependent; not all HyperSDK chains qualify for this subsector.
Practitioner Validation Check: If Ethereum-anchored HyperSDK deployments were removed, teams seeking custom VM appchains with Ethereum settlement/security would need to build bespoke execution and settlement logic.
Underlying Rollup Base: Custom execution VM with Ethereum anchoring via settlement or security bridges (not a native rollup engine).
Level of Protocol Abstraction: High — VM templates, networking, and consensus primitives provided.
Bespoke Engineering Required: Moderate — protocol engineering avoided, but VM logic must be defined.
Execution Environment Options: Custom VM (non-EVM by default; EVM-like behavior must be explicitly implemented).
Configurable Parameters: State model, transaction semantics, gas logic, block production rules, fee mechanics.
Sequencer Model Options: Chain-defined block production (single or multi-producer depending on design).
Upgrade Model: Chain-defined upgrades, governed by deployer-chosen governance.
Settlement Layer: Ethereum L1 (via settlement or security anchoring mechanisms).
Security Inheritance: Partial and configurable — depends on how Ethereum anchoring is implemented (not inherent like rollups).
Fault / Validity Proof Inheritance: None by default — HyperSDK chains do not natively inherit rollup-style fraud or validity proofs.
Isolation vs Shared Security: Fully isolated execution; shared security only if explicitly engineered.
Does This Enable L3s: Yes — HyperSDK chains can function as L3-style appchains when anchored to Ethereum.
Failure Propagation Model: Appchain failures do not propagate automatically; settlement anchoring defines recovery paths.
Latency Trade-offs: Very high throughput and low latency at the cost of weaker native Ethereum coupling.
Framework Ownership: Developed and maintained by Avalanche Labs.
Who Controls Upgrades: Chain deployers fully control upgrades and governance.
Emergency Controls: Defined at the chain level; no enforced framework-level safeguards.
Path to Sovereignty: High — chains are highly sovereign by design.
Operational Complexity: High — teams must manage VM logic, infrastructure, and Ethereum anchoring.
Fixed vs Variable Costs: High fixed engineering and infra costs; low marginal execution costs.
Infrastructure Responsibility Split: Primarily on chain deployer; Avalanche provides SDK only.
Vendor Lock-in Risk: Low-to-moderate — SDK dependency, but execution logic is custom-owned.
Number of Chains Deployed: Limited for Ethereum-anchored variants; HyperSDK adoption stronger in non-Ethereum contexts.
Types of Users: Advanced teams needing custom execution semantics.
Ecosystem Alignment: Stronger alignment with Avalanche ecosystem; Ethereum anchoring is secondary.
Dependency Concentration Risk: Moderate dependency on Avalanche tooling and SDK evolution.
Composability with Base Rollup: Not applicable — interaction occurs via settlement/bridges.
Cross-Rollup Messaging Assumptions: Requires external messaging or bridge infrastructure.

Description: A rollup deployment platform that enables teams to launch Ethereum-anchored rollups and appchains using existing rollup frameworks (e.g., OP Stack, Arbitrum Nitro, ZK stacks) without managing low-level protocol engineering or infrastructure.
Reason of inclusion: Standardizes and abstracts the rollup deployment pipeline—configuration, infrastructure, and lifecycle management—allowing teams to launch Ethereum-settled chains without building or operating rollup protocol logic themselves.
Practitioner's Note: Caldera is best evaluated as “rollups-as-a-service”: it does not define rollup mechanics, but it meaningfully lowers the barrier to deploying and operating them.
Practitioner Validation Check: If Caldera were removed, many teams would need to directly integrate OP Stack, Nitro, or ZK frameworks and operate infra in-house to launch Ethereum-anchored chains.
Underlying Rollup Base: Configurable: OP Stack, Arbitrum Nitro, and selected ZK rollup frameworks.
Level of Protocol Abstraction: Very high — protocol logic is inherited; deployers focus on configuration.
Bespoke Engineering Required: Minimal — primarily parameter selection and application integration.
Configurable Parameters: Gas model, block time, fee routing, sequencer setup, DA options (framework-dependent).
Sequencer Model Options: Inherited from base framework; operated or coordinated via Caldera.
Upgrade Model: Framework upgrades flow from the underlying stack; deployer controls application-level upgrades.
Settlement Layer: Ethereum L1 (directly or indirectly via the chosen rollup framework).
Security Inheritance: Inherited entirely from the selected rollup stack (optimistic or ZK).
Fault / Validity Proof Inheritance: Inherited from OP Stack, Nitro, or ZK framework used.
Isolation vs Shared Security: Execution isolated per chain; security assumptions shared with upstream framework.
Does This Enable L3s: Yes — supports L3-style appchains when deployed on top of L2 rollups.
Base Layer Dependency: Ethereum L1 via chosen L2 / rollup framework.
Failure Propagation Model: Appchain → base rollup → Ethereum, depending on topology.
Latency Trade-offs: Lower fees and faster UX with additional settlement layers.
Who Controls Upgrades: Protocol upgrades controlled by upstream framework governance; deployers control appchain configuration.
Emergency Controls: Operational safeguards provided by Caldera; ultimate authority depends on framework and deployer setup.
Path to Sovereignty: Moderate — deployers gain operational control but remain dependent on Caldera and underlying frameworks.
Operational Complexity: Low-to-medium — significantly reduced versus self-operated rollups.
Fixed vs Variable Costs: Recurring platform fees plus variable costs tied to usage and L1 data posting.
Infrastructure Responsibility Split: Caldera manages infra; deployers manage applications and governance choices.
Vendor Lock-in Risk: Moderate — migration requires re-deploying or re-operating the rollup independently.
Number of Chains Deployed: Multiple production and announced rollups across gaming, DeFi, and consumer apps.
Types of Users: Application teams prioritizing speed-to-market over protocol ownership.
Ecosystem Alignment: Strong alignment with OP Stack and Arbitrum ecosystems.
Dependency Concentration Risk: Dependency on Caldera’s platform and supported framework roadmap.
Native Interoperability Support: Inherited from the underlying rollup framework.
Composability with Base Rollup: Asynchronous composability via base rollup and Ethereum settlement.
Cross-Rollup Messaging Assumptions: Framework-dependent; typically external messaging layers required.
External Bridge Dependency: Yes — required for interoperability beyond the chosen ecosystem.

Description: A rollup deployment and infrastructure platform that enables teams to launch and operate Ethereum-anchored rollups and appchains (primarily OP Stack–based) without running core infrastructure themselves.
Reason of inclusion: Standardizes and operationalizes the rollup launch lifecycle—deployment, sequencing, data availability integration, upgrades, and monitoring—allowing teams to ship Ethereum-settled chains without bespoke protocol or infra engineering.
Practitioner's Note: Conduit is best evaluated as “managed rollup infrastructure”, not a framework defining execution or settlement logic. It abstracts ops, not protocol design.
Practitioner Validation Check: If Conduit were removed, teams would need to self-operate OP Stack (or equivalent) infrastructure to launch and maintain Ethereum-anchored rollups.
Type of Framework: Rollup deployment platform / managed infrastructure layer.
Level of Protocol Abstraction: Very high — deployers interact with configuration, not protocol internals.
Bespoke Engineering Required: Minimal — application integration and parameter selection only.
Configurable Parameters: Gas pricing, block time, fee routing, sequencer configuration, DA provider selection.
Sequencer Model Options: Single sequencer operated/managed via Conduit; decentralization depends on OP Stack roadmap.
Upgrade Model: Framework upgrades follow OP Stack evolution; deployers manage app-level upgrades.
Settlement Layer: Ethereum L1 (direct settlement via OP Stack).
Security Inheritance: Full Ethereum settlement security under optimistic assumptions.
Fault / Validity Proof Inheritance: Inherits OP Stack fraud-proof and challenge-window model.
Isolation vs Shared Security: Execution isolated per chain; security assumptions shared with OP Stack.
Does This Enable L3s: Yes — supports L3-style appchains when deployed on top of OP Stack L2s.
Base Layer Dependency: Ethereum L1 or OP Stack L2s (deployment-dependent).
Failure Propagation Model: L3 → L2 → L1, depending on topology.
Latency Trade-offs: Lower fees and faster UX with additional settlement hops.
Who Controls Upgrades: Core protocol upgrades driven by OP Stack governance; deployers control chain configuration.
Emergency Controls: Operational safeguards and incident response handled by Conduit; ultimate authority depends on OP Stack and deployer governance.
Path to Sovereignty: Low-to-moderate — strong operational dependence on Conduit and OP Stack.
Operational Complexity: Low — Conduit handles infra, monitoring, and ops.
Fixed vs Variable Costs: Recurring platform fees plus variable costs tied to usage and L1 posting.
Infrastructure Responsibility Split: Conduit manages infra; deployers manage apps and governance decisions.
Vendor Lock-in Risk: Moderate — migration requires standing up self-hosted OP Stack infra.
Number of Chains Deployed: Multiple production OP Stack–based chains launched via Conduit.
Types of Users: Application teams prioritizing speed, reliability, and managed ops.
Ecosystem Alignment: Strong alignment with OP Stack / Superchain ecosystem.
Dependency Concentration Risk: High dependency on Conduit operations and OP Stack roadmap.
Native Interoperability Support: Inherited from OP Stack / Superchain standards.
Composability with Base Rollup: Asynchronous composability with Ethereum and OP Stack peers.
Cross-Rollup Messaging Assumptions: Relies on OP Stack messaging patterns and external layers.
External Bridge Dependency: Yes — required for interoperability outside OP Stack ecosystem.
